meta.titre: Answer a literal reading comprehension question in one's own words

sections.contenu_markdown: A literal comprehension question always has its answer written somewhere in the passage - the real skill being tested is not guessing, but locating that information precisely and expressing it clearly in your own words.

items: Skimming a passage quickly to locate the relevant paragraph
Basic sentence construction to reformulate an idea

sections.contenu_markdown:
A literal question asks about information that is DIRECTLY stated in the passage (facts, events, reasons explicitly given), as opposed to an inference question (which requires reading between the lines). To answer it correctly: locate the relevant part of the passage (often signalled by a keyword from the question), identify the exact information requested, then REFORMULATE it in your own words rather than copying the sentence word-for-word - unless the instruction explicitly allows quoting.

A complete answer should include every element the question asks for, not just part of it: if a question asks "why", a full cause-and-effect explanation is expected, not a single isolated word.
sections.formule_principale: \text{Complete answer} = \text{locate the information} + \text{reformulate in one's own words} + \text{include every element asked}

sections.enonce_markdown: Passage extract: "Ngozi missed the school bus because she had overslept after staying up late to finish an assignment." Question: Why did Ngozi miss the school bus?

etapes.action: Locate the relevant information in the passage
etapes.justification: The keyword "missed the school bus" directly matches the question.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Located sentence: "Ngozi missed the school bus because she had overslept after staying up late to finish an assignment."

etapes.action: Identify every element of the cause
etapes.justification: The passage gives a two-step cause: staying up late, which led to oversleeping.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Two linked causes: staying up late to finish an assignment → oversleeping

etapes.action: Reformulate the answer in one's own words
etapes.justification: The answer should not simply copy the sentence verbatim.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Ngozi missed the bus because she woke up late, having gone to bed late the previous night while completing a piece of schoolwork.

sections.conclusion_markdown: A complete literal answer restates BOTH linked causes (staying up late AND oversleeping as a result), reformulated in different words from the original passage, rather than a partial answer mentioning only one of the two.

items.erreur_markdown: Copying the exact sentence from the passage word-for-word as the answer.
items.pourquoi_faux: Most comprehension exercises explicitly ask for answers "in your own words as far as possible": copying demonstrates that a sentence was located, but not that its meaning was genuinely understood and could be reformulated.
items.correction_markdown: Always rephrase the located information using different words and sentence structure, unless direct quotation is explicitly requested.

items.erreur_markdown: Giving only part of the requested information (e.g. only "she overslept", omitting the reason why she overslept).
items.pourquoi_faux: A full "why" question, when the passage gives a chain of causes, expects the complete chain to be reported, not just its final link.
items.correction_markdown: Before finalising an answer, check the passage again to confirm no additional relevant detail related to the question has been left out.

items.enonce_markdown: Passage extract: "The market was unusually crowded on Saturday because a big football match was being broadcast on a giant screen nearby." Question: Why was the market unusually crowded on Saturday?
items.solution_markdown: The market was crowded because a football match was being shown on a large screen close by, attracting extra people to the area.

items.enonce_markdown: Explain, in general terms, why simply quoting a sentence from a passage is usually considered an incomplete answer to a comprehension question, even if the quoted sentence is correct.
items.solution_markdown: Quoting a sentence only shows that the relevant information was located in the passage; it does not demonstrate that the reader has genuinely understood its meaning well enough to express it independently. Comprehension exercises specifically test this deeper understanding, which is why reformulating the answer in one's own words is usually explicitly required and rewarded, while direct copying is penalised even when the content itself is correct.

items.enonce_markdown: A comprehension question asks "What THREE reasons does the writer give for the town's water shortage?" but a candidate's answer only mentions two reasons found in the passage. Explain what mark this answer would likely receive and why, and what the candidate should have done differently.
items.solution_markdown: This answer would likely receive only partial credit, since the question explicitly asks for THREE reasons and only two are provided: markers typically award marks per correct element identified, so omitting one third of the requested information directly reduces the score, even if the two reasons given are accurate. The candidate should have reread the relevant section of the passage more carefully (or reread the question to note the specific number requested) to ensure all three reasons were located and included before finalising the answer.

items_markdown: A literal question's answer is directly stated in the passage - the task is to locate and reformulate it, not to guess.
Always reformulate in your own words rather than copying the passage verbatim, unless quoting is explicitly allowed.
Include every element the question asks for (all causes, all reasons, exact numbers requested).
Reread the question's exact wording (how many? why? what?) before finalising an answer, to avoid omitting part of what is asked.
